section.title: The Promised Rest
section.sectionRationale: The writer completes the second warning by developing the theme of rest. Because the wilderness generation failed to enter, and because David spoke of 'today' long after Joshua, a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God. The section ends with the searching word of God that exposes every heart, sharpening the call to enter by faith.
section.thesis: The rest God promised was not exhausted by Canaan or by Joshua, for God still says 'today'; a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, entered by faith and not by unbelief, and the living, penetrating word of God lays every heart bare before the One to whom we must give account.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the promise of rest still open, forfeited only by unbelief; the proof from Scripture that a Sabbath rest remains beyond Joshua's day; and the call to strive to enter, under the exposing gaze of God's living word.

units.label: The promise of rest still stands

verses.text: Therefore, while the promise of entering His {{katapausis|rest}} still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it.
For we also received the good news just as they did; but the message they heard was of no value to them, since they did not share the {{pistis|faith}} of those who comprehended it.

Now we who have believed enter that rest. As for the others, it is just as God has said: “So I swore on oath in My anger, ‘They shall never enter My rest.’” And yet His works have been finished since the foundation of the world.

units.label: A Sabbath rest still remains
units.note: beyond Joshua, God still says today

verses.text: For somewhere He has spoken about the seventh day in this manner: “And on the seventh day God rested from all His works.”
And again, as He says in the passage above: “They shall never enter My rest.”
Since, then, it remains for some to enter His rest, and since those who formerly heard the good news did not enter because of their disobedience,
God again designated a certain day as “Today,” when a long time later He spoke through David as was just stated: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.
There remains, then, a {{sabbatismos|Sabbath rest}} for the people of God.
For whoever enters God’s rest also rests from his own work, just as God did from His.

units.label: Strive to enter, under the living word

verses.text: Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one will fall by following the same pattern of disobedience.

For the {{logos|word}} of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight; everything is uncovered and exposed before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account.

katapausis.gloss: Rest, the settled repose God promised. The writer shows it means far more than the land of Canaan: it is God's own rest, begun at creation and still open, into which believers enter through faith in Christ.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust. The good news must be joined with faith to profit the hearer; the wilderness generation heard but did not believe, while those who believe enter the rest. Faith is the door into God's rest.

sabbatismos.gloss: A Sabbath rest, a Sabbath keeping. A rare word coined to name the rest that remains for God's people, patterned on God's own resting on the seventh day, a ceasing from self-effort into the finished work of God.

logos.gloss: Word, message, the utterance of God. God's word is living and active, sharper than a sword, piercing to the deepest divisions of a person and judging the heart's thoughts, so that no one can hide from the God who speaks.

basic.context: The writer keeps developing the idea of rest. The wilderness generation failed to enter Canaan, but that was not the whole of God's rest. Centuries after Joshua led Israel into the land, God still spoke through David of a 'today' to enter His rest. So a Sabbath rest still remains, a ceasing from our own works into God's finished work, entered by faith. The passage closes with the piercing word of God that sees everything.
basic.hermeneutics: The argument is careful biblical reasoning: God rested on the seventh day; He barred the rebels from His rest; He later still says 'today'; therefore the rest remains open. Read rest here as God's own rest, deeper than a place, entered by trusting Christ's finished work.
basic.originalLanguages: The key word katapausis, rest, is deepened by the rare sabbatismos, a Sabbath keeping. The rest is entered by pistis, faith, not unbelief. And the section ends with the logos, the living word of God that exposes the heart.
basic.typology: Canaan and Joshua's conquest were shadows of a greater rest. God's seventh-day rest at creation is the pattern. Both point to the rest fulfilled in Christ, in whom we cease from striving to save ourselves.
basic.christ: Jesus, whose name in Greek is the same as Joshua, gives the true rest Joshua could not. In Him we rest from our own works, trusting His finished work of purifying sins and sitting down at God's right hand.
basic.god: God rested on the seventh day and invites His people into His own rest. He speaks a living word that reads every heart, and He is the One to whom we must give account, holy and all-seeing.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2 records God resting on the seventh day. Psalm 95 supplies the 'today'. Matthew 11 records Jesus' invitation, come to Me and I will give you rest.
basic.oneStory: From creation's Sabbath, through Canaan and its failure, the theme of rest runs forward to the rest that remains in Christ, and on to the eternal rest of the people of God.

context.literary:
The passage is the second half of a sermon on Psalm 95, and it is the most tightly argued stretch in the letter. Its single word is 'rest', which is pressed into service in verses 1, 3, 5, 6, 10 and 11, and the argument depends on setting two Old Testament texts side by side because they share it. Genesis 2:2 in verse 4 says God rested on the seventh day. Psalm 95:11 in verses 3 and 5 says the unbelieving would never enter His rest. The writer lets the two sayings explain each other. A Jewish teacher would call the method linking by a shared word, and it was a respected way of reading Scripture: if the same word turns up in two places, each place sheds light on the other.

The movement runs in five steps. Verses 1 and 2 give the alarm: the promise stands, so be careful. Verses 3 to 5 give the first proof: believers enter, unbelievers do not, and God's own rest has been available since creation. Verses 6 to 8 give the second proof from the timing: if Israel had received the rest under Joshua, David would not centuries later speak of 'another day'. Verses 9 and 10 draw the conclusion, which is the only place in the New Testament where the word 'Sabbath rest' appears. Verse 11 turns the conclusion into a command, and verses 12 and 13 close the entire unit, begun at 3:7, with a picture of God's word as a sword and of God Himself as the Judge to whom all must answer.

Two small structural features deserve notice. The passage begins with 'fallen short' in verse 1 and ends its exhortation with 'fall' in verse 11, so the warning frames the argument. And the closing verse plays on a word: God's 'word' that cuts in verse 12 is matched by the 'account' we must give in verse 13, which in Greek is also logos. The reader who has been addressed by God's word will be asked to answer for what he did with it.
context.historical:
For Israel the Sabbath was the central sign of the covenant. It looked back to creation, Exodus 20:11 and 31:17, and, in Deuteronomy's version of the commandment, to the exodus, since Israel had been a slave in Egypt and was now to give rest to everyone in the house, Deuteronomy 5:12-15. A Jewish believer would have heard in the word 'rest' a whole world of belonging: the weekly day, the land, and the peace God had promised.

The land was the next layer. Deuteronomy 12:9-10 says the people had not yet come to the resting place and inheritance, and that it would come when they crossed the Jordan and God gave them rest from all their enemies. When Joshua had completed the conquest, the record says the LORD gave them rest on every side and that not one good promise had failed, Joshua 21:44-45. Joshua 23:1 says it was a long time after the LORD had given Israel rest. The writer to the Hebrews does not deny any of this. He takes it seriously enough to ask a sharp question: if that was all God had meant, why did a psalm written long after the conquest speak of entering the rest as still future? The book of Judges makes the point clearer. The generation that followed Joshua did not know the LORD, Judges 2:10-12, and the settled peace of the land was fragile.

Hebrews says the psalm came 'through David', verse 7, as the Greek version of the psalm also heads it. David reigned several centuries after Joshua, and in his time the ark had been brought to Jerusalem, a 'resting place' for God, Psalm 132:7-8 and 13-14. Yet even then, Psalm 95 was sung with 'Today' still open.

The first readers were tired. They had heard the good news, but pressure and delay were wearing them down, and the writer says with real pastoral feeling that he fears some may be judged to have fallen short. The wilderness generation had also heard the good news, and he will not let his readers assume that hearing is the same as believing.
context.canonical:
The theme of rest runs from the first chapter of the Bible to the last. In Genesis 2:2-3 God completes His work, rests on the seventh day, blesses it and makes it holy. The commandment to keep the Sabbath in Exodus 20:8-11 grounds it in that example. After the exodus, God promises Moses, 'My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest', Exodus 33:14, which makes rest a gift of His presence and not merely a break from labour. Deuteronomy looks forward to the resting place in the land, Joshua records its partial arrival, and the Psalms keep the hope alive: Psalm 132:13-14 calls Zion God's resting place forever, and Isaiah 11:10 says the Root of Jesse's 'place of rest will be glorious'. Jeremiah 6:16 invites the people to walk in the ancient paths and find 'rest for your souls', and Isaiah 28:12 records the offer of rest to the weary, which was refused.

The New Testament connects the theme to Christ. Jesus says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest', Matthew 11:28, taking up the words of Jeremiah 6:16 and making Himself the place where rest is found. Paul tells the Colossians that Sabbaths are a shadow of things to come, but the body that casts the shadow belongs to Christ, Colossians 2:16-17. Within Hebrews, the rest of 4:9-10 is tied to the finished work of the Priest who 'sat down at the right hand of God' after offering one sacrifice, 10:11-14, in contrast with the priests who stand day after day. And the book of Revelation speaks of those who die in the Lord resting from their labors, Revelation 14:13.

The second half of the passage has its own canonical history. The word of God as a sword appears in Isaiah 49:2, where the Servant's mouth is a sharp sword, and in Ephesians 6:17, where the sword of the Spirit is the word of God. In Revelation 1:16 and 19:15 a sharp sword comes from the mouth of the risen Christ, so the word that searches the heart in Hebrews 4:12 is the word of the One who will judge.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants his readers to hear a promise and a warning together, and he builds them from the same word. The promise is that God's rest is still open: a long time after Joshua, God was still saying 'Today'. The warning is that open does not mean automatic. The wilderness generation heard good news and failed to enter, so the readers must not think that merely having heard it is enough.

He also wants to lift their eyes from the land to the One who made the rest. The argument from Genesis 2:2 takes the reader back to God's own Sabbath, so that the rest of which the psalm speaks is not a geographic prize but a share in the peace God Himself enjoys after finishing His work. That is why he can say that whoever enters it 'rests from his own work, just as God did from His'. The readers, who are tempted to retreat into systems of effort and observance, are meant to see that the rest is entered by trusting a finished work.

The last two verses show his pastoral hand at its sharpest. After the long argument, he leaves the readers standing before the word of God and before God Himself. He is not content to win a point about the Old Testament. He wants them to take the matter personally and to ask what is in their own hearts.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The reasoning from Genesis, Psalm 95 and Joshua is description. It sets out what God said and when, and it draws a conclusion about what remains. It does not tell the reader to keep any particular day or to adopt any ritual. The prescriptions are in the exhortations: be careful, verse 1; make every effort to enter, verse 11. Both verbs speak of urgency and not of a rule for hours or days.

Care is needed with verse 10. It describes the person who has entered God's rest as resting from his own work. It does not forbid ordinary work or praise idleness. The rest in view is rest from trying to secure standing with God by effort. The command to make every effort in verse 11 shows that faith is an active thing, though its activity is that of a person running to the place of rest, not of a person earning it. Nor is verse 12 a licence to treat Scripture as a weapon to wield against others. It describes what God's word does to the one who hears it.

debates.question: What is the 'rest' that remains for the people of God?

views.label: God's own rest, entered now by faith and completed in glory
views.case: The rest is patterned on God's seventh-day rest and received as believers cease relying on their own works and trust the finished work of Christ. Verse 3 says 'we who have believed enter that rest', in the present tense, and verse 11 says make every effort to enter, so the rest is both begun and still ahead.

views.label: Chiefly the future, heavenly rest
views.case: Some stress that the rest is the final repose of the age to come. The pilgrim language of the letter, such as the city 'whose architect and builder is God', Hebrews 11:10, and Revelation 14:13, points this way, and verse 9 says it 'remains'.

views.label: Salvation itself, viewed as the end of striving
views.case: Others take rest as another picture of salvation, like the 'rest for your souls' of Matthew 11:29. The wording is flexible, and the writer pulls together creation, land and heaven in one image.

debates.bearing: On any of these readings the rest is God's gift, entered by faith in Christ and not by effort, and the summons is to enter it and not to be left outside it.

debates.question: How can the readers 'make every effort' to enter a rest received by faith?

views.label: Diligent perseverance in faith
views.case: The effort is not earning the rest but continuing in the trust that receives it. The Greek word means to be eager and diligent, and 6:11 asks for the same diligence 'to the very end'. Paul speaks in the same way when he says God works in us to will and to act while we work out our salvation, Philippians 2:12-13.

views.label: A warning against a faith that does nothing
views.case: Others emphasise that the verse is aimed at spiritual sluggishness. The people who failed in the wilderness failed because they would not move forward in trust, so the effort called for is to obey the word when it is spoken, and not to let the day pass.

debates.bearing: The two views agree that the effort is the energy of trust, not a rival to it. The rest is entered by faith, and faith is the kind of thing that hurries toward its object.

debates.question: Does the 'Sabbath rest' of verse 9 require believers to keep a weekly Sabbath?

views.label: The weekly Sabbath continues as a sign of the rest
views.case: The word sabbatismos is related to the verb for keeping the Sabbath, and some hold that the weekly day continues as a regular sign and foretaste of the rest to come, observed on the seventh day or on the first day of the week.

views.label: The rest is fulfilled in Christ and the day is a shadow
views.case: Paul says a Sabbath is a shadow of things to come and that the body belongs to Christ, Colossians 2:16-17, and Romans 14:5 leaves the observance of days to conscience. On this view Hebrews 4 does not impose a day but announces the reality the day pointed to.

debates.bearing: The passage itself gives no command about a day. Its concern is the reality to which every Sabbath pointed, and that reality is entered by trust in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with a verb that the BSB softens. The Greek is phobethomen, 'let us fear', from the ordinary word for fear. The writer is not recommending terror but the reverent alarm that a sensible person feels at the edge of a cliff. The same family of word returns in 12:28, where believers are to worship with 'reverence and awe'. Fear here is a kind of wisdom, the right response to a promise that can be missed.

The phrase 'deemed to have fallen short' is dokei hysterekenai. The first word means 'seem' or 'be judged', so the clause can be heard as seeming to have come too late, or as being found to have missed it. The second, hysteréo, means to lag behind or to fall short, and it comes again in 12:15, 'See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God'. The verb is in the perfect tense, which presents a failure as a standing result. The writer is thinking of the final verdict on a life.

Verse 2 says that 'we also received the good news just as they did'. The Greek verb is euangelizo, to bring good news, so the writer is saying that Israel in the wilderness was evangelised: they too were told of a promised rest. The next clause is difficult, and the BSB footnote says 'literally not having been united in the faith of those who heard'. Manuscripts differ. One reading says the message was not united with faith in those who heard it, the other says the hearers were not united by faith with those who listened and believed, meaning Joshua and Caleb. Both agree that hearing without believing is empty.

In verse 3 the tenses matter. 'We who have believed' is an aorist participle, referring to the act of believing, and 'enter' is present: eiserchometha. The believer has believed and is entering. In verse 10 the tense reverses. 'Whoever enters' is an aorist participle, and 'rests' is also aorist, 'has also rested', so the rest is seen from the end as completed: the one who has come in has ceased from his own works as God ceased from His.

Verse 8 names Joshua, and the Greek reads Iesous, the very form of the name used of Jesus. Greek readers, who only knew the name as Iesous, could hardly miss the play. The verb for the rest Joshua gave is in the same family as the noun in the psalm, katapauo, which is the verb Greek Joshua uses when the LORD gives rest to the people, as in Joshua 1:13. The writer is asking whether Joshua's gift could be what Psalm 95 meant, and answers that it could not.

Verse 9 uses sabbatismos, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It is formed from the verb sabbatizo, to keep a Sabbath, a verb the Greek Old Testament uses of Israel keeping the day, as in Exodus 16:30. The ending turns it into a noun of action, a Sabbath-keeping. The writer chooses a different word from the psalm's katapausis, perhaps to link the rest of the psalm with the Sabbath of Genesis.

Verse 11 asks for spoudasomen, a verb of eager diligence, and warns against 'the same pattern of disobedience'. The word for pattern is hypodeigma, which can mean a model to copy or a copy of something, as in 8:5. Here it is a negative example.

In verses 12 and 13 the vocabulary is sharp. 'Living' and 'active' are zon and energes, from which we get energy. The sword is machaira distomos, a double-mouthed blade. 'Thoughts and intentions' are enthymesis and ennoia, the deliberations and the purposes of the heart. 'Uncovered' is gymna, naked, and 'exposed' is a perfect participle of trachelizo, a verb tied to the neck, trachelos. Ancient readers took it of a wrestler's hold on the neck, or of a victim's head bent back for the knife, and either way it pictures someone laid helplessly open. The last clause says literally 'with whom is our word', logos again, which means the account we must give.

typology.fulfillment: God finished His work and rested, and the writer says His works have been finished since the foundation of the world, verse 3. Israel's Sabbath day imitated that rest, Exodus 20:11. The fulfillment comes in Christ, who offered one sacrifice for sins and then 'sat down at the right hand of God', Hebrews 10:12, in contrast to the priests who stand every day. On the cross He said 'It is finished', John 19:30. Believers share in that finished work and rest from their own. The type falls short as a weekly pause that must be repeated, while the work of Christ is done once for all, Hebrews 9:12.

Joshua led Israel into the land and the LORD gave them rest on every side, Joshua 21:44. The writer argues that this rest could not have been the whole, since David later spoke of another day. Joshua carries the name that in Greek is Jesus, and in Christ the leader and the rest are joined. He leads His people into the rest that Joshua's land only foreshadowed. The type falls short because the land could be lost, as the book of Judges and the exile show, and because Joshua could not give an inward rest from sin and fear.

The Sabbath was a sign between God and Israel, a permanent covenant. It ordered the week around a day of ceasing from work and trusting God to provide. Paul says Sabbaths are a shadow, with the substance in Christ, Colossians 2:16-17. Hebrews says a sabbatismos remains, a rest that the day pointed to. In Christ the sign gives way to the reality of ceasing from self-justification and finding rest for the soul, Matthew 11:28-29. The type falls short because it could mark rest but could not give it.

After the golden calf, the LORD told Moses that His presence would go with him and that He would give him rest. Here rest and presence are joined: rest is not first a place but the company of God. In Christ, God is with His people, and the invitation is to come to Him, Matthew 11:28. The final form appears in Revelation 21:3, where God dwells with man. The type falls short because Moses had to climb a mountain to meet Him, while Christ comes to the weary where they are.

study.christ:
The passage does not name Jesus until the Greek name appears in disguise in verse 8, but everything in it points to Him. The first way it does so is by the name itself. Joshua, who led Israel into the land, bears in Greek the name Iesous, and the writer's question, 'if Joshua had given them rest', puts two leaders of the same name side by side. Joshua led a generation across the Jordan, yet God was still speaking about another day. The One who leads His people into the rest that was always intended is Jesus. The name was given to Him because He will save His people from their sins, Matthew 1:21, and the salvation is a salvation into rest.

The second way is by invitation. The words of Jesus in Matthew 11:28-30 are the answer to this chapter's search. He says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest', and adds that His yoke is easy and His burden light. Jeremiah 6:16 had described rest for the soul as something found on the ancient path, and Jesus puts Himself at the centre of that path. The rest the psalm promised is no longer a place to be reached by obedience to a code; it is given by the One who is gentle and humble in heart.

The third way is by the finished work. Verse 10 says that the one who enters God's rest rests from his own work, as God did from His. The letter will unpack this in terms of the Priest who offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down, Hebrews 10:11-14. A priest in the old order never sat, because his work was never done. Christ sits because His work is finished, and those who trust Him are invited to stop trying to finish it themselves. This is the heart of what Paul says in Ephesians 2:8-9, that salvation is by grace through faith, 'not by works, so that no one can boast', and in Romans 4:4-5, that faith is credited as righteousness to the one who does not work but believes.

The fourth way is by the living word. The word of God in verse 12 is not an impersonal force. Hebrews opened by saying that God has spoken by His Son, 1:2, and the New Testament calls the Son the Word, John 1:1. Revelation 1:16 pictures a sharp two-edged sword coming from the mouth of the risen Lord, and 19:15 shows the same sword at the judgment. So the word that exposes the heart is the voice of the One before whom we stand. This is a frightening picture until we notice what comes next in the letter. The One who sees everything is the great high priest who sympathizes with our weakness, 4:14-16, and the exposure that would be terrible before a stranger becomes a place of mercy before Him.

There is a limit to the reading. The text does not turn every detail of Canaan into a picture of Jesus. The identification of Joshua with Jesus rests on a shared name that the writer himself uses, and the rest is anchored by the New Testament's own words about Christ's invitation and finished work.
study.god:
The passage shows God first as the One who rests, and that is a surprising thing to say about the Creator. The seventh-day rest in Genesis 2:2 does not mean He was tired. It means He had completed His work, and the writer takes the point that His works have been finished since the foundation of the world. God is not anxiously striving to bring His purposes to pass. He has already done what He set out to do and now invites His creatures into the peace that follows. A God who rests is a God who is secure, and His invitation to rest is an invitation to share that security.

He is the God who keeps a promise open. The writer's argument depends on the fact that God still said 'Today' through David, centuries after Joshua. The offer was not withdrawn when Israel failed, nor exhausted when they reached the land. This reveals a patience that waits through whole eras and a faithfulness that does not forget what it has sworn. Hebrews will later say that when God wanted to make the unchanging nature of His purpose clear, He guaranteed it with an oath, 6:17.

He is the God who judges unbelief. The oath quoted in verses 3 and 5 is still in force for those who disobey. The passage does not soften it. God is angry at the faithlessness of people He has rescued, and He does not pretend that hearing the message is the same as believing it. His justice and His invitation are held together, so that the warning is itself a form of the invitation.

He is the God who speaks and who sees. Verse 12 describes His word as living and active, penetrating soul and spirit, joints and marrow, and judging the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Verse 13 says nothing is hidden from His sight and everything is uncovered. This is the omniscience of Psalm 139:1-4, where the LORD knows our words before they are on our tongue. It is sobering, since no pretence survives it, but it also means that God is never deceived about the people who truly trust Him.

Finally, He is the God to whom we must give account. The last phrase of the passage reminds the readers that there is a Judge. The attributes of God shown here, His rest, patience, justice and knowledge, are not separate. They belong to one holy and loving Person. For worship, this means that the right response is reverent gladness. The believer comes to God without self-defence, because He already knows everything, and without fear, because the rest He offers is real. The passage teaches us to take God's promise seriously and His word seriously, and to bring our hearts into the open before Him.

crossReferences.note: The first Sabbath. God finishes His work, rests, blesses the seventh day and sets it apart. Hebrews quotes verse 2 in verse 4 and builds on it. Notice that the account has no evening and morning for the seventh day, which fits the writer's picture of a rest that is still open and not tied to a single day.

The Sabbath is made a permanent sign between God and Israel because He made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh. This is the background to the word 'Sabbath rest', and it shows how closely Israel linked its weekly rhythm with the work of creation.

Moses says Israel has not yet come to the resting place and inheritance, and that it will come when they cross the Jordan and God gives them rest from their enemies. It shows that rest in the land was a promise with a condition and a future, which is what the writer builds on when he says the rest is still ahead.

The record of Joshua's day: the LORD gave Israel rest on every side and not one good promise failed. This is the strongest evidence for the view that Joshua had given rest, and Hebrews takes it seriously before arguing that the psalm still speaks of another day.

The LORD has chosen Zion and says 'This is My resting place forever and ever'. It shows rest as God's own, a place where He dwells. It supports the thought that the rest of Hebrews 4 is first God's and that His people share it by being with Him.

God's answer to Moses after the golden calf: 'My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.' Rest here is bound to God's company. It adds depth to the idea that the rest of Hebrews 4 is communion with God and not merely a place.

Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest and to take His yoke. The invitation echoes Jeremiah 6:16, and it is the gospel form of what Hebrews 4 argues. The rest is in a Person, and it is received by coming and learning from Him.

The priests of the old order stand day after day, but this Priest offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down. It gives the ground of the rest in 4:10. The finished work of Christ is why believers can cease from their own.

Paul says Sabbaths are a shadow of things to come and that the body belongs to Christ. It shows how the New Testament reads the Sabbath: as a sign pointing ahead, now fulfilled in Him. It fits the claim that a sabbatismos remains and that its substance is Christ.

By grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast. It states plainly what Hebrews 4:10 says in a picture: the one who has entered God's rest has ceased from his own works. Paul adds that we are created for good works, so the rest is not idleness.

The LORD has searched and known His servant, understands his thoughts from afar and knows a word before it is spoken. It is the Old Testament counterpart of Hebrews 4:13. Where the letter stresses the exposure of everything before God, the psalmist treats the same knowledge as intimacy.

A voice from heaven says that those who die in the Lord will rest from their labors, and their deeds will follow them. It looks ahead to the completion of the rest of Hebrews 4, and shows that rest from labour does not mean the loss of what was done in faith.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible opens with God at rest. He has made a world that is very good, He has made humanity in His image, and on the seventh day He ceases from His work and blesses the day. The picture is of a finished creation in which people are meant to share God's own peace. Then sin enters, and the story becomes the search for the way back. The ground is cursed, labour becomes toil, and humanity is driven out of the garden. The rest of Eden becomes the memory that the rest of the Bible pursues.

Israel's story gives the search a shape. The people are freed from slavery in Egypt and led toward a place of rest. The Sabbath is given as a weekly sign, a day of ceasing that tells a people who were once slaves that they are now free. The land is the promised resting place, and Joshua's conquest gives it in part. Yet the wilderness generation fails, the book of Judges shows a rest that is fragile, and the exile will drive the people out of the land again. The psalm keeps sounding its 'Today', and the prophets keep holding out a rest that has not yet come.

Hebrews 4 says that the rest has been found in Christ. The Joshua who leads His people in is Jesus, and the rest He gives is the rest of the finished work. The long story of striving, of sacrifices that never ended and priests who never sat, comes to an end in One who offered a single sacrifice and sat down. The people who trust Him cease from their own works and enter, in measure now, a rest that the Sabbath and the land had only pointed to. That is the place in the story where the church lives: between the rest begun and the rest completed, still hearing the word 'Today' and still called to make every effort not to fall.

The story looks ahead to the day of full entry. Revelation 14:13 promises rest from labor to those who die in the Lord, and Revelation 21:3-4 describes the dwelling of God with man, where every tear is wiped away and there is no more death. The creation that was blessed on the seventh day is made new, the exile is over, and the people of God enter the rest He prepared from the foundation of the world. The word that searched the heart in Hebrews 4 becomes the voice that welcomes the weary home.

quiz.q: Why does the writer say a rest still remains for God's people?

options.text: Because God still said 'today' through David long after Joshua, so Joshua's conquest was not the final rest.
options.note: Verses 7 to 9 make exactly this argument.

options.text: Because Israel never entered Canaan at all.
options.note: Israel did enter under Joshua; the point is that this was not the ultimate rest.

options.text: Because God has grown tired and needs rest.
options.note: The rest is God's gift to His people, not a divine need.

options.text: Because the Sabbath day was abolished.
options.note: The argument builds on the Sabbath pattern, not its abolition.

options.text: By faith, ceasing from our own works and trusting God's finished work.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 and 10 tie entry to faith and resting from our works.

options.text: By working harder to earn it.
options.note: The rest is a ceasing from self-effort, received by faith.
Joshua's conquest could not give the true rest; it comes by faith.

options.text: By keeping the seventh day perfectly.
options.note: The Sabbath is the pattern, but the rest is entered by faith in Christ, not ritual perfection.

quiz.q: What is said about the word of God in verses 12 to 13?

options.text: It is living and active, piercing the heart and exposing everything before God.
options.note: The word judges thoughts and intentions; nothing is hidden from God.

options.text: It is a dead letter with no present power.
options.note: It is explicitly living and active.

options.text: It concerns only outward behaviour, not the heart.
options.note: It reaches the thoughts and intentions of the heart itself.
The warning is addressed to the readers themselves, to whom all is uncovered.

quiz.q: What does 'make every effort to enter that rest' mean?

options.text: Persevere diligently in faith, not falling by the same unbelief as the wilderness generation.
options.note: Verse 11 links effort to avoiding the pattern of disobedience.

options.text: Earn the rest by good works.
options.note: The rest is received by faith, not earned.

options.text: Relax and do nothing at all.
options.note: The call is to strenuous perseverance in faith, not passivity.
It is persevering faith, not attained perfection, that is in view.

questions: The rest of God is a ceasing from our own works. Where are you still striving to earn what Christ has already finished?
The good news profits only when joined with faith. Is there truth you have heard but not truly trusted?
God's word pierces to the thoughts and intentions of the heart. How do you respond to being fully known by God, with nothing hidden?
We are told to make every effort to enter the rest. What does diligent, persevering faith look like in your life this season?
Jesus gives the rest that Joshua could not. What burden could you lay down today by trusting His finished work?

translationNotes.note: The name rendered 'Joshua' is the same word as 'Jesus' in Greek; the wordplay quietly points beyond Joshua to the greater one who gives true rest.
'Sabbath rest' renders the rare word sabbatismos, a Sabbath keeping, coined to distinguish this abiding rest from mere cessation and to tie it to God's own seventh-day rest.
'Word of God' here refers to God's living utterance and message; the imagery of the two-edged sword stresses its power to divide and to judge the inner person.
